Part 1: The peripheral nervous system

slides.title: Part 1: The peripheral nervous system

Part 1: The peripheral nervous system

Peripheral nervous system

primarily deals with

primarily deals with

Peripheral nervous system. Adapted from: Christinelmiller, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes:
The peripheral nervous system is not as contained as the central nervous system because it is defined as all parts of the nervous system that are not the central nervous system. In describing the anatomy of the peripheral nervous system, it is necessary to describe the common structures, the sensory and motor neurons and the ganglia, as they are found in various parts of the body. 

Recall that the peripheral nervous system can be divided into the somatic nervous system, consisting primarily of voluntary control over skeletal muscle and those muscle interactions with the external environment, and the autonomic nervous system, which consists primarily of unconscious regulation of internal body processes, many of which act to maintain homeostasis. A third division, the enteric nervous system, which deals with digestive system function, is often included within the autonomic nervous system.

Let’s first examine a few of the components of the peripheral nervous system in detail, and then we will get into the somatic and autonomic nervous systems.

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes:
Ganglia

A ganglion is a group of neuron cell bodies in the periphery. Ganglia can be categorized, for the most part, as either sensory ganglia or autonomic ganglia, referring to their primary functions. The most common type of sensory ganglion is a dorsal root ganglion. These ganglia are the cell bodies of afferent neurons with axons that are sensory endings in the periphery, such as in the skin, and that extend into the central nervous system through the dorsal nerve root.

The other major category of ganglia, those of the autonomic nervous system, will be examined later in this chapter.

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes:
Nerves

Bundles of axons in the peripheral nervous system are referred to as nerves. Afferent nerves bring sensory information from the peripheral nervous system into the central nervous system, while efferent nerves send motor output from the central nervous system to the peripheral nervous system.

Nerves in the periphery are different than their central counterparts, called tracts. Nerves are composed of more than just nervous tissue. They have connective tissues invested in their structure, as well as blood vessels supplying the tissues with nourishment. Nerves are associated with the region of the central nervous system to which they are connected, either as cranial nerves (12 pairs) connected to the brain or spinal nerves (31 pairs) connected to the spinal cord.

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes:
The cranial nerves are primarily responsible for the sensory and motor functions of the head and neck, although one of these nerves, the vagus, cranial nerve ten, targets organs in the thoracic and abdominal cavities as part of the parasympathetic nervous system. Cranial nerves can be classified as sensory nerves, motor nerves, or a combination of both.

Traditionally, 12 pairs of cranial nerves have been described, numbered from 1-12. Mnemonic phrases have been developed to help students memorize these. A traditional phrase, whose words begin with the same letters as the cranial nerves is: “On Old Olympus’ Towering Tops, A Finn And German Viewed Some Hops”. Another version is: “Oh, Once One Takes The Anatomy Final, Very Good Vacations Are Here!”.

However, even though it was described more than a century ago, one cranial nerve was missed in this list, and it is now given the number zero, so it is known as CN0, or cranial nerve 0. Let’s look at these 13 cranial nerves in more detail.

slides.notes: CN0, the terminal nerve, is a small nerve located adjacent to CN1, the olfactory nerve, at the anterior inferior surface of the brain. CN2, the optic nerve, is also located in this region anterior to the brain stem. All three of these nerves are sensory nerves. While the olfactory nerve senses olfactory stimuli (smells), the terminal nerve is connected to parts of the brain that regulate reproductive hormones, and it is thought that this nerve senses pheromones, chemical signals released between individuals, and is subconsciously processed by the brain. The optic nerve is responsible for our sense of sight.

slides.notes: The four remaining cranial nerves shown here, all have mixed afferent and efferent function. That is, some of their neurons are sensory, while others are motor. The trigeminal nerve, CN5, provides facial sensations, while also regulating mastication (chewing). The facial nerve, CN7, provides taste input from some parts of the tongue, while also regulating the muscles producing facial expressions. The glossopharyngeal nerve provides sensory information regarding taste, head and neck somatosensation, blood pressure, and the concentration of dissolved gasses in the blood; in terms of its motor functions, it helps with salivary gland secretion and swallowing. The vagus nerve, CN10, is a major sensorimotor nerve that provides information about, and helps to regulate, organs of the digestive, respiratory, and cardiovascular systems. It is also the main nerve of the parasympathetic division of the autonomic nervous system.

Somatic nervous system
voluntary responses to processed sensory information

From Unit 15: The Functional Organization of the Nervous System. The diagram represents the divisions of the nervous system involved in each of the basic functions: sensation (receiving and processing information from the external and internal environment), integration (comparing the sensory input with stored information and with other sensory inputs in order for the body to react appropriately) and response (most commonly, a motor command generated by the somatic nervous system or the autonomic nervous system).

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes: The somatic nervous system is responsible for our voluntary responses to information relayed to the central nervous system by the sensory system. That response is executed by means of skeletal muscle contraction.

slides.title: Part 2: The somatic nervous system
slides.body:
Part 2: The somatic nervous system

Reflex
neurons and neural pathways responsible for a reflex action constitute the reflex arc
stretch reflex – nervous system responds to the stretching of a muscle (the stimulus) with contraction of that same muscle (the response)
helps to maintain posture and balance
e.g., patellar reflex (or knee-jerk reflex):
sensory input
tap of patellar tendon stretches quadriceps muscle
central processing
sensory neurons synapse onto and stimulate motor neuron in spinal cord
motor output
motor neuron stimulates quadriceps muscle contraction (leg extension)

The Patellar Reflex. The stimulus (stretching of the quadriceps muscle caused by tapping on the tendon) triggers a nerve impulse in a sensory neuron, which synapses with and stimulated a motor neuron, leading to the contraction of the quadriceps. (credit: www.backyardbrains.com/experiments/Musclekneejerk, protected under Creative Commons License)

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes:
The distinction between the structures of the peripheral and central nervous systems can most easily be demonstrated through a simple reflex, an automatic response that the nervous system produces in response to specific stimuli. The neurons and neural pathways responsible for a reflex action constitute the reflex arc. One of the simplest reflex acts is the stretch reflex, by which the nervous system responds to the stretching of a muscle (the stimulus) with contraction of that same muscle (the response). This response protects the muscle from over-stretching, but more importantly, it has a crucial role in maintaining posture and balance. 

The patellar reflex (or knee-jerk reflex) is an example of stretch reflex and it occurs through the following steps:

-Tapping of the patellar tendon with a hammer causes the stretching of muscle fibres in the quadriceps muscle, which stimulates sensory neurons innervating those fibres.
-In the sensory neuron, a nerve impulse (sn action potential) is generated, which travels along the sensory nerve fibre from the muscle, through the dorsal root ganglion, to the spinal cord.
-The sensory neuron stimulates a motor neuron in the ventral horn of the spinal cord.
-That motor neuron sends a nerve impulse (an action potential) along its axon.
-This impulse reaches the quadriceps muscle, causing its contraction and the extension of the leg (a kick).

slides.title: Part 2: The somatic nervous system
slides.body:
Part 2: The somatic nervous system

Reflex
neurons and neural pathways responsible for a reflex action constitute the reflex arc
withdrawal reflex – e.g., pulling hand away from hot stove:
sensory input 
sensory neurons send an AP through dorsal root to spinal cord
central processing
sensory neuron synapses on motor neuron
motor output
stimulated motor neuron sends AP to biceps brachii, causing muscle contraction and forearm flexion

Withdrawal reflex. Credit: MartaAguayo, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes:
Another example of a simple spinal reflex is the withdrawal reflex, which occurs, for example, when you touch a hot stove and pull your hand away. This reflex occurs through a similar sequence of steps:


-Sensory receptors in the skin sense extreme temperature and the early signs of tissue damage.
-In a sensory neuron, a nerve impulse is generated, which travels along the sensory nerve fibre from the skin, through the dorsal root ganglion, to the spinal cord.
-The sensory neuron stimulates a motor neuron in the ventral horn of the spinal cord.
-That motor neuron sends a nerve impulse along its axon.
-This impulse reaches the biceps brachii, causing contraction of the muscle and flexion of the forearm at the elbow to withdraw the hand from the hot stove.

The basic withdrawal reflex includes sensory input (the painful stimulus), central processing (the synapse in the spinal cord), and motor output (activation of a ventral motor neuron that causes contraction of the biceps brachii).

slides.title: Part 2: The somatic nervous system
slides.body:
Part 2: The somatic nervous system

Reflex
neurons and neural pathways responsible for a reflex action constitute the reflex arc
withdrawal reflex can be accompanied by cross extension – counterbalancing movements on the other side of the body
e.g., ipsilateral synaptic connections stimulating flexor muscles on the same side of the body & contralateral synaptic connections stimulating extensor muscles on the other side of the body
reflex arc in figure also involves interneurons, between sensory and motor neurons

Cross extension reflex. Credit: Cenveo, CC BY 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes: A more complex reflex accompanying a withdrawal reflex is cross extension: counterbalancing movement on the other side of the body by stimulation of the extensor muscles in the contralateral limb. Hence, the ipsilateral motor neuron stimulates flexor muscles on the same side of the body, while the contralataral motor neuron stimulates extensor muscles on the other side of the body. The reflex arc shown here also involves interneurons, which act as an intermediary between the sensory and motor neurons.

slides.title: Part 2: The somatic nervous system
slides.body:
Part 2: The somatic nervous system

Voluntary movement
conscious movements of body
e.g., reading this text:
sensory input
retina stimulated by light, projects to thalamus, then to occipital lobe of cerebral cortex
central processing
occipital lobe processes the information, in conjunction with dorsal stream in parietal lobe and ventral stream in temporal lobe
motor output
frontal lobe plans next eye movements, stimulates motor neurons in brain stem, cause movement of the extraocular muscles through 3rd, 4th, and 6th cranial nerves

Cranial nerves. Credit: OpenStax, CC BY 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

Cranial nerves of the eye. Credit: Romano, N., Federici, M. & Castaldi, A., CC BY 4.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes: The somatic nervous system also controls voluntary movement and more complex motor functions. For example, reading the text on the screen starts with visual sensory input to the retina, which then projects to the thalamus, and on to the occipital lobe of the cerebral cortex. The occipital lobe processes the information, in conjunction with the dorsal visual stream regions in the parietal lobe and the ventral visual stream in regions of the temporal lobe, resulting in the conscious perception of these letters and understanding of the content. As you continue reading, regions of the cerebral cortex in the frontal lobe plan how to move the eyes to follow the lines of text. The output from the cortex causes activity in motor neurons in the brain stem that cause movement of the extraocular muscles through the third, fourth, and sixth cranial nerves. This example also includes sensory input (the retinal projection to the thalamus), central processing (the thalamus and subsequent cortical activity), and motor output (activation of neurons in the brain stem that lead to coordinated contraction of extraocular muscles).

slides.title: Part 3: The somatic nervous system
slides.body:
Part 3: The somatic nervous system

Autonomic nervous system
involuntary responses to processed sensory information
regulation of internal organs
regulated via hormones and neurotransmitters
2 divisions:
sympathetic
fight or flight
parasympathetic
rest and digest

From Unit 15: The Functional Organization of the Nervous System. The diagram represents the divisions of the nervous system involved in each of the basic functions: sensation (receiving and processing information from the external and internal environment), integration (comparing the sensory input with stored information and with other sensory inputs in order for the body to react appropriately) and response (most commonly, a motor command generated by the somatic nervous system or the autonomic nervous system).

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes:
The autonomic nervous system is responsible for our involuntary responses to information relayed to the central nervous system by the sensory system. That response is regulated by means of hormones and neurotransmitters. 

The autonomic nervous system regulates many of the internal organs through a balance of two aspects, or divisions. In addition to the endocrine system, the autonomic nervous system is instrumental in regulating homeostatic mechanisms in the body. The two divisions of the autonomic nervous system are the sympathetic division and the parasympathetic division. The sympathetic system is associated with the “fight-or-flight” response, and parasympathetic activity is referred to by the epithet of “rest and digest”.

slides.title: Part 3: The autonomic nervous system
slides.body:
Part 3: The autonomic nervous system

Sympathetic division
“fight or flight: response evolved for situations such as confrontation of or escape from a predator
in modern era, can be stimulated by benign factors such as exams, horror movies, watching sports
In such stressful situations, you may experience:
adrenaline (epinephrine) floods circulatory system
heart rate increases
sweat glands activate
bronchi of the lungs dilate
pupils dilate
blood pressure increases
blood vessels in skeletal muscles dilate

Warning, run away. Credit: Neoclassical_Velocity.JPG: Unitfreakderivative work: Nevit Dilmen, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes:
Imagine that you are in a stressful situation. Adrenaline (formally called epinephrine in most countries) starts to flood your circulatory system. Your heart rate increases. Sweat glands become active. The bronchi of the lungs dilate to allow more air exchange. Pupils dilate to increase visual information. Blood pressure increases in general, and blood vessels in skeletal muscles dilate to allow more blood flow to those muscles. Time to run. Time to fight. 

The sympathetic division of the autonomic nervous system, or sympathetic system for short, evolved for animals to deal with situations such as escape from a predator. Humans have inherited this system from our ancestors and in the modern era, it can even be triggered by more benign stimuli like classroom exams, horror movies, or watching your favorite sports team on television.

slides.title: Part 3: The autonomic nervous system
slides.body:
Part 3: The autonomic nervous system

Sympathetic division
These changes involve multiple systems regulated in coordinated manner
respiratory system
increased oxygen intake
cardiovascular system
increased delivery of oxygen and nutrients to muscles
musculoskeletal system
fighting or running away
integumentary system
sweat keeps body from overheating
smooth muscle
blood flow to GI tract diverted to brain and skeletal muscles
pupils dilate to see danger

Sympathetic nervous system. Credit: http://www.scientificanimations.com, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes: To respond to a threat—to fight or to run away—the sympathetic system causes divergent effects as many different effector organs are activated together for a common purpose. More oxygen needs to be inhaled and delivered to skeletal muscle. The respiratory, cardiovascular, and musculoskeletal systems are all activated together. Additionally, sweating keeps the excess heat that comes from muscle contraction from causing the body to overheat. The digestive system shuts down so that blood is not absorbing nutrients when it should be delivering oxygen to skeletal muscles. To coordinate all these responses, the connections in the sympathetic system diverge from a limited region of the central nervous system to a wide array of ganglia that project to the many effector organs simultaneously. The complex set of structures that compose the output of the sympathetic system make it possible for these disparate effectors to come together in a coordinated, systemic change.

Sympathetic division
thoracolumbar system

Sympathetic nervous system. Credit: Blausen.com staff (2014). "Medical gallery of Blausen Medical 2014". WikiJournal of Medicine 1 (2). DOI:10.15347/wjm/2014.010. ISSN 2002-4436., CC BY 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

Part 3: The autonomic nervous system

Sympathetic division
central neuron in the lateral horn of any of these spinal regions projects to ganglia adjacent to the vertebral column through the ventral spinal roots
majority of sympathetic ganglia belong to network of sympathetic chain ganglia that runs alongside vertebral column

Sympathetic nervous system. Credit: Laboratoires Servier, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

Cross-section of Spinal Cord (from Unit 15).

slides.notes: A central neuron in the lateral horn of any of these spinal regions projects to ganglia adjacent to the vertebral column through the ventral spinal roots. The majority of ganglia of the sympathetic system belong to a network of sympathetic chain ganglia that runs alongside the vertebral column. The ganglia appear as a series of clusters of neurons linked by axonal bridges.

slides.title: Part 3: The autonomic nervous system
slides.body:
Part 3: The autonomic nervous system

Sympathetic division
preganglionic fibre
axon from central (preganglionic) neuron
short in sympathetic division
postganglionic fibre
axon from a ganglionic neuron (a.k.a. postganglionic neuron) to target
adrenal medulla
specialized ganglionic neuron that acts as an endocrine gland
interior portion of the adrenal gland

& NE

Somatic and autonomic nervous system neurons. Adapted from : Daniel Walsh and Alan Sved, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes:
An axon from the central neuron that projects to a sympathetic ganglion is referred to as a preganglionic fibre or neuron, and represents the output from the central nervous system to the ganglion. Because the sympathetic ganglia are adjacent to the vertebral column, preganglionic sympathetic fibres are relatively short. A postganglionic fibre—the axon from a ganglionic neuron that projects to the target effector—represents the output of a ganglion that directly influences the organ. Compared with the preganglionic fibres, postganglionic sympathetic fibres are long because of the relatively greater distance from the ganglion to the target effector. (Note that the term “postganglionic neuron” may be used to describe the projection from a ganglion to the target. The problem with that usage is that the cell body is in the ganglion, and only the fibre is postganglionic. Typically, the term neuron applies to the entire cell.)

One type of ganglionic neuron has become specialized in that rather than acting as a typical neuron and releasing a neurotransmitter at a synapse, it instead acts like a gland, and releases its chemical messenger into the bloodstream. This relay involves axons from central sympathetic neurons projecting to the adrenal medulla, a modified ganglion that forms the interior portion of the adrenal gland.

slides.title: Part 3: The autonomic nervous system
slides.body:
Part 3: The autonomic nervous system

Sympathetic division
projections diverge widely through body
preganglionic fibres branch; branches can split and target:
adjacent chain ganglion
lower or higher chain ganglia
collateral ganglia outside of chain ganglion
adrenal medulla
one preganglionic neuron can thus target many effectors

The Sympathetic Division of the Autonomic Nervous System. Neurons from the lateral horn of the spinal cord (preganglionic nerve fibers – solid lines)) project to the chain ganglia on either side of the vertebral column or to collateral (prevertebral) ganglia that are anterior to the vertebral column in the abdominal cavity. Axons from these ganglionic neurons (postganglionic nerve fibers – dotted lines) then project to target effectors throughout the body. (The names of specific ganglia and nerves, as well as their target organs, are not examinable material in this course.)

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes:
The projections of the sympathetic division of the autonomic nervous system diverge widely, resulting in a broad influence of this system on the body. This divergence is seen in the branching patterns of preganglionic sympathetic neurons, whose branches can synapse on a neuron in the adjacent chain ganglion, while other branches extend up or down to a different level of the chain ganglia, and yet other branches will pass through the chain ganglia and project through to a collateral ganglion or to the adrenal medulla. All of these branches mean that one preganglionic neuron can influence different regions of the sympathetic system very broadly, by acting on widely distributed organs.

Please note that this figure is a different version of the one on slide 21. They show the same information, but the drawing is different. Hopefully having two versions will help you visualize this system better than having just one.

slides.title: Part 3: The autonomic nervous system
slides.body:
Part 3: The autonomic nervous system

Parasympathetic division
central neurons located on either side of thoracolumbar region of the spinal cord (para- = “beside” or “near”)
usually more active than sympathetic
many similar effectors targeted but effects usually opposite of sympathetic:
decrease respiratory activity
decreased cardiovascular function
decreased musculoskeletal system tone & energy mobilization
increased digestive activity
increased urinary activity
reproductive systems regulated by both sympathetic and parasympathetic systems

Parasympathetic nervous system. Credit: Blausen.com staff (2014). "Medical gallery of Blausen Medical 2014". WikiJournal of Medicine 1 (2). DOI:10.15347/wjm/2014.010. ISSN 2002-4436., CC BY 3.0 , via Wikimedia Commons

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes:
When not responding to an immediate threat, the “rest and digest” parasympathetic system is generally more active than the sympathetic system.  Many of the same effectors in the body are innervated by both divisions of the autonomic nervous system, but activation of each division tends to have opposing effects.  Sympathetic system activation tends to increase activity in the respiratory, cardiovascular, and musculoskeletal systems while reducing activity in the digestive system.  Parasympathetic system activation on the other hand tends to decrease activity in the respiratory, cardiovascular, and musculoskeletal systems while increasing activity in the digestive and urinary systems. Reproductive systems are regulated by both sympathetic and parasympathetic activation. Generally speaking, the activity of the many organs that receive input from both systems is dependent on whether neurons of the parasympathetic or sympathetic system are releasing more of their neurotransmitter onto each organ at a given time.

The parasympathetic division of the autonomic nervous system is named so because its central neurons are located on either side of the thoracolumbar region of the spinal cord (para- = “beside” or “near”). The parasympathetic system can also be referred to as the craniosacral system (or outflow) because the preganglionic neurons are located in nuclei of the brain stem and the lateral horn of the sacral spinal cord.

slides.title: Part 3: The autonomic nervous system
slides.body:
Part 3: The autonomic nervous system

Parasympathetic division
preganglionic fibres
from cranial region travel in cranial nerves
from sacral region travel in spinal nerves
ganglia called terminal ganglia because located right at (or within) target organs

The Parasympathetic Division of the Autonomic Nervous System. Neurons from brain-stem nuclei, or from the lateral horn of the sacral spinal cord, project to terminal ganglia near or within the various organs of the body. Axons from these ganglionic neurons then project the short distance to those target effectors. (The names of specific ganglia and nerves, as well as their target organs, are not examinable material in this course.)

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes: The connections, or “circuits,” of the parasympathetic division are similar to the general layout of the sympathetic division with a few specific differences. The preganglionic fibres from the cranial region travel in cranial nerves, whereas preganglionic fibres from the sacral region travel in spinal nerves. The targets of these fibers are terminal ganglia, which are located near – or even within – the target organ. The postganglionic fibre thus projects from the terminal ganglia only a short distance to the effector.

slides.title: Part 3: The autonomic nervous system
slides.body:
Part 3: The autonomic nervous system

Parasympathetic division
preganglionic fibres longer than in sympathetic division
postganglionic fibres shorter than in sympathetic division
Autonomic vs somatic
Somatic NS does not contain a relay ganglion

& NE

Somatic and autonomic nervous system neurons. Adapted from : Daniel Walsh and Alan Sved, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes:
Comparing the relative lengths of axons in the parasympathetic system, the preganglionic fibres are long and the postganglionic fibres are short because the ganglia are close to – and sometimes within – the target effectors. This is in contrast to the sympathetic system, where it was the preganglionic fibres that were short, and the postganglionic fibres that were long.

It is also a good idea to compare both of the autonomic nervous system motor neuron relays, with signaling through the somatic nervous system. If you recall, in contrast to the autonomic nervous system, the somatic motor neurons did not possess any relay ganglia at all – there was a direct connection of a nerve from the spinal cord to the target skeletal muscle.

slides.title: Part 3: The autonomic nervous system
slides.body:
Part 3: The autonomic nervous system

Chemical signaling in ANS
cholinergic receptors bind acetylcholine (ACh)
adrenergic receptors bind norepinephrine (NE, a.k.a. noradrenaline) and epinephrine (Epi, a.k.a., adrenaline)

& NE

Somatic and autonomic nervous system neurons. Adapted from : Daniel Walsh and Alan Sved, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes:
Where an autonomic neuron connects with a target, there is a synapse. The electrical signal of the action potential causes the release of a signaling molecule, which will bind to receptor proteins on the target cell. Synapses of the autonomic system are classified as either cholinergic, meaning that acetylcholine is released, or adrenergic, meaning that norepinephrine and/or epinephrine are released. The terms cholinergic and adrenergic refer not only to the signaling molecule that is released but also to the class of receptors that each binds.

The term adrenergic should remind you of the word adrenaline. Adrenaline and epinephrine are two names for the same molecule. The adrenal gland (in Latin, ad- = “on top of”; renal = “kidney”) secretes adrenaline. The ending “-ine” refers to the chemical being derived, or extracted, from the adrenal gland. A similar construction from Greek instead of Latin results in the word epinephrine (epi- = “above”; nephr- = “kidney”). In scientific usage, epinephrine is preferred in the United States and Canada, whereas adrenaline is preferred in Great Britain, because “adrenalin” was once a registered, proprietary drug name in the United States. Though the drug is no longer sold, the convention of referring to this molecule by the two different names persists. Similarly, norepinephrine and noradrenaline are two names for the same molecule.

slides.title: Part 3: The autonomic nervous system
slides.body:
Part 3: The autonomic nervous system

Chemical signaling in ANS (and SNS)
all preganglionic fibres (and SNS motor neurons) release ACh
targets at skeletal muscle and ganglia is always a nicotinic type of cholinergic receptor
targets of parasympathetic postganglionic fibres possess muscarinic receptors
hence can be targeted by different pharmacological drugs
postganglionic sympathetic fibers usually release norepinephrine (or sometimes epinephrine)

& NE

Somatic and autonomic nervous system neurons. Adapted from : Daniel Walsh and Alan Sved, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes:
Note that all preganglionic fibres, both sympathetic and parasympathetic, as well as all somatic motor neurons release acetylcholine onto nicotinic receptors. So, all fibres leaving the spinal cord release acetylcholine onto nicotinic receptors.

The postganglionic parasympathetic fibres also release acetylcholine, but onto muscarinic receptors, a different type of cholinergic receptor. Having a different type of cholinergic receptor present at autonomic effectors is convenient when needing to prescribe medications to treat some of these targets, as it minimizes cross-reactivity. For instance, a drug that stimulates parasympathetic receptors on the heart to reduce heart rate will not simultaneously cause somatic muscle contraction, or stimulate ganglionic neurons that could activate the sympathetic nervous system and cause opposing responses.

Postganglionic sympathetic fibers usually release norepinephrine (or sometimes epinephrine) onto adrenergic receptors (except for fibers that project to sweat glands and to blood vessels associated with skeletal muscles, which release acetylcholine).

slides.title: Part 3: The autonomic nervous system
slides.body:
Part 3: The autonomic nervous system

Chemical signaling in ANS (and SNS)
neurotransmitters are released at a synapse & hormones are released into the blood
however, NE is released at both synapses and into the blood, so is considered both

& NE

Somatic and autonomic nervous system neurons. Adapted from: Daniel Walsh and Alan Sved, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes: Signaling molecules can belong to two broad groups. Neurotransmitters are released at synapses, whereas hormones are released into the bloodstream. These are simplistic definitions, but they can help to clarify this point. Acetylcholine can be considered a neurotransmitter because it is released by axons at synapses. The adrenergic system, however, presents a challenge. Postganglionic sympathetic fibres release norepinephrine, which can be considered a neurotransmitter. But the adrenal medulla releases epinephrine and norepinephrine into circulation, so they should be considered hormones. Thus, norepinephrine can be considered both a neurotransmitter and a hormone, depending on how it is released.

slides.notes: You may have noticed that the name nicotinic receptor sounds like nicotine, which can be found in tobacco products. Tobacco products have long been used by Indigenous cultures of North America, dating back for thousands of years. Many receptors are named after drugs that affect them. The understanding that some plant or fungal compounds can affect the body has long been understood in traditional cultures, long before these compounds were ever identified and named. These traditional uses have helped scientists to identify plants and fungi for analysis, which has then greatly enhanced our understanding of physiology and neuroscience.

slides.title: Part 4: Receptor pharmacology
slides.body:
Part 4: Receptor pharmacology

Nicotine (nicotinic agonist):
gives name to nicotinic receptors
affect somatic, sympathetic and parasympathetic circuits

& NE

Somatic and autonomic nervous system neurons. Adapted from : Daniel Walsh and Alan Sved, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes: Nicotine, the compound after which nicotinic receptors are named, is classified as an agonist of these receptors, because it increases the activation of those receptors. As you can see from this diagram, nicotine can affect muscle contraction via the somatic nervous system, such as causing shakiness of the hands. It can also affect both sympathetic and parasympathetic divisions of the autonomic nervous system in complex ways, to regulate various physiological processes. And, of course, it can also affect the brain directly, and can bind more strongly to the nicotinic receptor subtypes in the brain than those in skeletal muscle, which is one reason why nicotine is so very addictive.

slides.title: Part 4: Receptor pharmacology
slides.body:
Part 4: Receptor pharmacology

Curare (nicotinic antagonist) derived from South American liana vines
blocks nicotinic receptors at skeletal muscles and thus causes paralysis
used traditionally as poison on blow darts for hunting

Curare darts and quiver. Credit: Rama, CC BY-SA 3.0 FR, via Wikimedia Commons

A Yagua (Yahua) tribeman demonstrating the use of blowgun (blow dart), at one of the Amazonian islands near Iquitos, Peru. Credit: JialiangGao www.peace-on-earth.org, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

Liana vines, Ecuador. Credit: Hanspeter Bellers, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes: A nicotinic receptor antagonist, which binds strongly to the nicotinic receptor subtype in skeletal muscles is the compound curare. Curare is found in South American liana vines, and has traditionally been used Indigenous cultures in that region for hunting purposes. Curare blocks nicotinic receptors at skeletal muscles and thus causes muscle paralysis in prey; it is used as a poison on blow darts for hunting. It is therefore an antagonist to these receptors, because it blocks the endogenous ligand, acetylcholine, from binding to them.

Part 4: Receptor pharmacology

Muscarine (muscarinic agonist):
gives name to muscarinic receptors
derived from Amanita muscaria
can causes blurred vision + other smooth & cardiac muscle & neural effects, and at high doses: convulsions, & even death

Amanita muscaria mushrooms. Credit: Holger Krisp, CC BY 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes: Muscarinic receptors are named after muscarine, an agonist of muscarinic receptors. Muscarine is a compound derived from Amanita muscaria mushrooms. Muscarine can causes blurred vision via actions on smooth muscles in the eye. It can also affect other smooth & cardiac muscles, as well as the nervous system – which if affected by high doses can cause convulsions or even death.

slides.title: Part 4: Receptor pharmacology
slides.body:
Part 4: Receptor pharmacology

Atropine (muscarinic antagonist) is extracted from deadly nightshade (Atropa belladonna), mandrake, and other related plants
muscarinic receptor is parasympathetic cholinergic receptor at cardiac muscle – thus atropine used as heart medication to raise heart rate
also causes dilation of pupils at optometrist (smooth muscle)

Eye treated with dilating eye drops (Atropine). Credit: Spito, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

Mandrake root. Credit: D arckangel, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

Mandrake (Mandragora officinarum), scanned from 15th century manuscript Tacuinum Sanitatis. Credit: Unknown author, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes: An antagonist of muscarinic receptors is atropine, a compound derived from deadly mandrake, nightshade, and other related plants. Because of their shape, mandrake roots were often described in folklore as creatures under the ground, that will cry when pulled from the earth. Because the muscarinic receptor is the parasympathetic cholinergic receptor at cardiac muscle, atropine is used as heart medication to raise heart rate. Atropine can also cause dilation of pupils at the optometrist, via its effects on smooth muscles in the eyes.
